title: The Three Cuts of Mimosa Root Bark, and Who Each One Suits
summary: Powder, shredded bark and stripped root are one material cut three ways. Powder gives colour fastest and filters worst. Shredded sits in the middle and is what most regular dyers settle on. Stripped root keeps longest and asks for the most preparation before it is useful.
body: A first order is usually placed before anyone knows how they will actually work, which is why the same question arrives every week: which cut should I buy? The honest answer is that it depends on one thing you can decide in advance, which is whether you care more about speed or about getting more than one bath out of a bag.
## Start from the surface, not the label

All three cuts contain the same colour. What separates them is how much of the material meets the water at once. A chip of bark has an outside and an inside; milling it to powder turns almost all of it into outside. Everything a dyer notices about the three forms follows from that single fact, which is why it is worth understanding once rather than memorising a list of tips.
## Powder
Powder is for people in a hurry and for people running tests. Soaked overnight and brought up to temperature, it has usually given what it has within the hour.

The cost is at the other end of the process. Fine particles stay in suspension rather than settling, they lodge between the plies of a skein, and they leave dark specks that look like a fault in the dyeing rather than a bit of material that could be rinsed out. They also give up nearly everything on the first pass, so a second bath is rarely worth the water you heat for it.

Where powder earns its place: [small test skeins](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece), cold-process soap, and any job small enough that straining is a two-minute problem rather than an afternoon.
## Shredded bark

Shredded is the working cut. Colour comes out more slowly, which pushes you towards the long warm bath that produces the better purples anyway, and the material lifts out of the pot in one movement with a slotted spoon or a mesh bag.

It also holds something in reserve. A pound that has given a full-strength first bath will usually give a second at roughly half to two-thirds the depth, and sometimes a third after that. Measured per usable bath rather than per pound, it is the cheapest of the three.
## Stripped root

Whole stripped root is the least processed thing on the shelf, and it behaves accordingly. Less cut surface is exposed to air and damp, so it keeps longer than either of the other two: this is the cut to buy if you are stocking for a year rather than a season.

In exchange it asks for work. You will be breaking or cutting it down before it is useful, an overnight cold soak stops being optional, and a first bath wants more time than you expect. Most people who buy it either mill their own to a grind they prefer, or are holding material against a gap in supply.
## A way to decide in one line

| If your priority is | Buy | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Speed, and small quantities | Powder | Ready within an hour of reaching temperature |
| Several tones from one bag | Shredded | A reliable second bath, often a third |
| Storing for next year | Stripped root | Least cut surface, so the slowest to change |
| Even colour in soap | Powder | Fine enough to disperse without specks |
| Least straining | Stripped root | Lifts out whole |
## What does not change between them

The colour range is the same. So is the ratio: between fifty and a hundred grams of material for every hundred grams of dry fibre gives a full shade on wool whichever cut you use. And so is the temperature rule, because a boiled bath turns brown no matter how the material was cut.
## Buying a mix

There is no rule against using two cuts on one project, and a quarter pound of powder alongside a pound of shredded is the combination we see most often on repeat orders. The powder pays for itself on the first afternoon of testing; the shredded is what does the actual work once you know what you are aiming at.
## What this material is not

Everything described here is raw botanical material sold for dyeing, soap making and craft work. It is not food, it is not a supplement, and it is not for human consumption. Nothing on this page is a recommendation to put any of it in or on a body.

title: Why Particle Size Changes Everything in a Dye Pot
summary: Milling does not add colour to bark. It multiplies the surface where colour crosses into water, and that one change explains why powder works faster, strains harder, floats, spoils sooner and gives no second bath. Understand the mechanism once and the rest follows without a list.
body: Two bags of the same bark, cut differently, behave so differently in a pot that people assume they bought two different things. They did not. One number changed, and everything else in this article is a consequence of it.
## The mechanism

Colour leaves plant material at the boundary between the material and the water. Grind a chip into powder and you have not created any more colour: you have created enormously more boundary, because the inside of every fragment becomes an outside.
That is the whole explanation. What follows is what it looks like from the pot.
## It arrives sooner, and then it is finished

Powder that has soaked overnight is usually giving everything it has within an hour of reaching temperature; the same weight of coarse material may want three. This is useful when you are running a sequence of tests and want each bath ready quickly, and it is a nuisance when you wanted a long slow bath and the colour is spent before the fibre has settled into it.
The same speed is why the second bath disappears. Coarse material holds colour in reserve simply because water has not reached the middle of it yet. Powder has no middle.
## It stays where you do not want it

Coarse fragments sink or can be lifted out. Fine particles do neither: they stay suspended, they float as often as they settle, and decanting moves them along with the liquid. They find their way between the plies of a skein and dry there as dark flecks.

In practice this means powder needs a real filter rather than a careless pour, and it means the material wants to be held in a mesh bag from the start if the piece being dyed is anything you cannot rinse aggressively afterwards.
## It becomes airborne

Milled plant material lifts into the air when a bag is opened, weighed or tipped. That is true of flour, paprika and sawdust, and it is true here. It is a handling matter rather than anything peculiar to this species, and a fitted dust mask, a slow hand and a wiped bench cover it.
## It takes up damp faster

The surface that lets colour out also lets moisture in. Powder is the cut most punished by a humid cupboard: it cakes, and caked powder never disperses evenly again. Stripped root, at the other end of the scale, is the one that forgives a poor storage spot for longest.
## What does not change

Two things are worth stating because people assume otherwise. The palette is identical: powder reaches the same plums, burgundies and roses at the same percentages of fibre weight. And boiling browns it exactly as it browns a coarse bath, so a fast bath is not permission to rush the heat. If anything the temptation is stronger, because everything else about powder is quick.

title: What Tannins Do in a Dye Bath
summary: Tannins bind to protein and to metal ions. That single property explains why tannin-rich bark takes so strongly on wool and silk, why it needs help on cotton, why a pinch of iron darkens a whole pot, and why hard water quietly dulls a colour you had judged in the jar.
body: Most dyeing advice is a list of instructions with the reasons left out. Tannin is worth an exception, because one property of it explains four separate things that otherwise look unrelated.
## One property
Tannins are plant compounds that bind readily to two things: protein, and metal ions. Everything below is that sentence, applied.
## Why wool and silk take it so easily

Wool and silk are protein fibres. The tannin has something to hold onto the moment the fibre enters the bath, which is why a tannin-rich bark gives depth on them with nothing more than a clean alum mordant and patience.

It is also why these fibres are unforgiving of an uneven start. If part of a skein wetted out and part did not, the tannin binds where the water went, and you get the pale patches people blame on the bark.
## Why cotton and linen need more work

Plant fibres are cellulose. There is far less for tannin to bind to, which is why natural colour on cotton is famously weak and why the traditional recipes for it add a tannin step of their own before the mordant. You are effectively giving the cellulose a protein-like surface to work with.
If you are taking a bark colour onto cotton, expect to spend the extra step rather than expect the bark to behave like it does on wool.
## Why iron darkens so violently

Iron is a metal ion, and tannin binds metal ions. A quantity of iron that looks like nothing at all — one or two per cent of the fibre weight — will take a plum to a slate or charcoal in under a minute, because it is not tinting the fibre, it is reacting with what is already on it.

This is also why the depth you can reach with iron depends on how much colour is in the fibre to begin with. A skein dyed at a hundred per cent of its weight in bark moves dramatically; one dyed at thirty barely shifts.
## Why hard water dulls a shade

Hard water carries dissolved calcium and magnesium. Those are metal ions too, and they bind some of the tannin before your fibre ever gets a chance at it. The result is not a disaster, it is a quiet flattening: the same recipe, a shade greyer and less clear than the one you remember.

If your colours are consistently duller than your notes say they should be, test the water before you blame the material. Rainwater or filtered water for the dye bath is the cheapest experiment in this craft.
## The practical summary

| Observation | The tannin reason |
| --- | --- |
| Deep colour on wool and silk | Tannin binds protein |
| Weak colour on cotton without extra steps | Cellulose gives it little to bind to |
| A pinch of iron changes everything | Tannin binds metal ions |
| Dull results from the same recipe | Minerals in hard water bind it first |
## What this material is not

title: Testing a Dye Before You Commit a Fleece
summary: Ten grams of yarn answers in an afternoon what a whole fleece answers in a ruined week. Dye a set of small skeins from one bath, change one thing at a time, dry every sample before judging it, and write the batch code on the card. That card beats any published chart.
body: Nobody plans to waste a fleece. It happens because a colour that looked right in a warm wet skein dried two shades lighter and slightly browner, and by then there was no undyed fibre left to try again with.
A test card costs about an hour and roughly thirty grams of material.
## Use the cut that is fastest

This is the one job where powder is plainly the right choice. You want the bath ready quickly, you are working in quantities where straining is trivial, and you have no interest in a second bath from the same material.
## Ten grams, not one

Very small samples lie. A gram of fibre in a jar has a different ratio of water to material than a pot does, and it wets out differently. Ten grams is enough to behave like the real thing and small enough that a set of six costs almost nothing.
Mordant the whole set together, in one pot, so that the mordant is not one of the variables you are trying to read.
## Change one thing per sample
The discipline is the whole method. A useful set looks like this:

- **The control.** Bath as mixed, nothing added, lifted at the time you expect to use.
- **Half the time.** Same bath, lifted early.
- **Double the time.** Same bath, left long.
- **A weak alkaline after-bath.**
- **A weak acid after-bath.**
- **A brief dip in iron**, at one per cent of the fibre weight.
Six samples, one bath, one afternoon. Anything you change in pairs tells you nothing about which of the two did the work.
## Judge them dry, and in daylight

Wet fibre reads darker and more saturated than it will ever look again. Dry every sample fully before you decide anything, and look at them by a window rather than under a kitchen bulb, which pushes everything warm.
## Write the card
Pin the samples to stiff card and write, for each one: the fibre, the mordant and its percentage, the material and its percentage, what you changed, how long it sat, and the batch code from the bag.

That last item is the one everybody leaves off and the one that matters six months later. Bark is an agricultural product; two harvests are not identical, and when you want to reproduce a colour, knowing which batch produced it is half the answer.
## What the card is worth

A published chart tells you what somebody else's water, wool and thermometer did. Your card tells you what yours do. After two or three of them you stop guessing at quantities altogether, which is the point at which this craft becomes repeatable rather than lucky.

title: Storing Root Bark So It Lasts
summary: Bark does not expire on a date. It is spoiled by damp, heat and light, in that order. Sealed, dry, dark and at an even temperature, a bag holds its colour for years; in a garage that swings from freezing to forty degrees, powder cakes and a year is optimistic.
body: The question behind most storage questions is really: has this gone off? Bark rarely goes off in the way food does. It gets damp, it cakes, and in a bad spot it grows something. Each of those is avoidable with a container and a sensible shelf.
## Damp is the enemy that matters
Bark takes up moisture from the air. A bag that has absorbed it will cake, and caked powder never disperses evenly again: it clumps in the bath and gives blotchy colour no amount of stirring fixes.
Worse, damp plus warmth inside a sealed bag is how mould starts. Material that smells musty or shows any bloom belongs on the compost heap rather than in a pot, whatever it cost.
## Four conditions, in order of importance

| Condition | Why | What it looks like in a house |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sealed | Keeps humidity out | A jar with a gasket, or the original bag inside a tub |
| Dry | Stops caking and mould | Not the cupboard beside the kettle |
| Dark | Slows fading in the bag | A cupboard, a tin, an opaque tub |
| Even temperature | Avoids cycles of condensation | Not a garage that freezes and bakes |
## Which cut keeps longest

Stripped root keeps longest, because so little of it is cut surface. Shredded is next. Powder is the most vulnerable, for the same reason it works fastest: nearly all of it is surface, and surface is where moisture arrives.
If you are buying ahead for the year, buy the coarse cut and mill what you need as you go rather than storing a year of powder.
## Small habits that pay

- Write the form and the batch code on the container the day it arrives. Nobody remembers six months later, and the batch is half of why a colour came out the way it did.
- Keep a silica sachet in the jar if you live somewhere humid.
- Decant working quantities into a smaller jar so the main stock is not opened every session.
- Let a cold bag come up to room temperature before opening it, or moisture condenses on what is inside.
## How to tell it is still good

Good material smells faintly earthy and woody, pours loose, and shows its colour the moment it hits warm water. Doubtful material clumps, smells sour or musty, or sits on top of the water without wetting. When in doubt, run ten grams against a test skein before you commit a project to it.
